strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: personalized/subtle video emotion recognition with CLIP, where generic prompts and image-level TTA are insufficient.

Proposes a lightweight method (CLIP-AU) that uses AU text prompts and frozen CLIP encoders, avoiding LLM-generated prompts and full CLIP fine-tuning; designs a temporal 1D-CNN/GLU module and AU adapter.

Introduces CLIP-AUTT with entropy-guided temporal window selection and AU prompt tuning for unsupervised test-time adaptation, which is conceptually reasonable for temporally evolving subtle expressions.

Evaluates on three subtle-expression datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH) and compares against multiple CLIP-based FER and TTA baselines; includes subject-wise results and ablations on window length, prompt type, AU adapter, and robustness.
Provides code in supplementary, implementation details, AU list, prompt templates, and qualitative visualizations, which supports reproducibility in principle.
Reported gains over CLIP-AU and TTA baselines are substantial in several settings, especially on BioVid and StressID, and the method is computationally efficient.
The core idea of using structured AU descriptions as textual prompts rather than class names or LLM captions is well motivated for fine-grained expression analysis.
weaknesses: The AU prompt set is inconsistent and appears technically incorrect. The main text describes AU-06 as 'cheek raiser' and AU-25 as 'lips part', while the supplementary table lists AU06 as 'eyelids_tightened' and AU25 as 'eyes_elitted_narrow_eye_opening'; many entries (head turn, eye turn, etc.) are not standard FACS AUs. This directly undermines the core claim of AU-guided fine-grained semantics and the method's interpretability.

CLIP-AUTT is framed as subject-level personalization, but it adapts independently per video and resets parameters afterward. It does not accumulate subject-specific information across multiple videos, so it is closer to transductive video-level test-time adaptation than personalization; the central claim of subject-specific adaptation is not adequately supported.

The TTA objective is risky: entropy minimization with batch size 1 on the lowest-entropy temporal window can reinforce incorrect confident predictions and cause class collapse. There is no pseudo-label filtering, consistency regularization, diversity term, or analysis of failure modes, yet very large gains (e.g., +14 WAR on StressID) are reported without explanation or statistical testing.

Critical controls are missing. There is no random/shuffled AU prompt baseline to show that AU semantics specifically matter beyond having 46 diverse text prompts; no quantitative AU agreement metric with OpenFace or ground-truth AUs; and no comparison to video-level TTA methods or image TTA methods properly adapted with temporal aggregation.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair to TTA methods: image-based TTA baselines are applied to videos without the proposed temporal module, and T3AL is adapted from temporal action localization to classification. This makes the reported margins difficult to attribute to the proposed method rather than to baseline mismatch.

Several results are suspiciously perfect (e.g., 100.0 WAR/F1 for multiple subjects) and target sets are small (10 subjects) with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed runs. On BAH, UAR is approximately chance (~50) for CLIP-AUTT, so the claimed robustness on hard personalization is not convincing.

Evidence for AU interpretability is qualitative and weak: the visual comparison with OpenFace is not quantified, and the classifier can learn an arbitrary mapping from prompt-similarity features, so alignment with true AU activations is not guaranteed.

The manuscript has clarity/reproducibility issues: inconsistent AU descriptions between main text and supplement, typos ('eyes_elitted', 'lip_hite'), duplicate figure captions, and insufficient detail on target subject splits, number of videos per subject, and whether adaptation and evaluation use the same videos.

strengths: The use of Action Unit (AU) descriptions as structured text prompts for CLIP is a promising direction for fine-grained facial expression recognition, providing a potential bridge between muscle-level semantics and vision-language models.

The paper presents a complete pipeline with two methods (CLIP-AU and CLIP-AUTT) and evaluates them on three challenging video-based subtle emotion datasets, showing consistent improvements over several baselines.
The adaptation is lightweight, tuning only AU text embeddings during test time, which is efficient and preserves the frozen CLIP encoders.
Extensive experiments include subject-wise analysis, ablations on temporal window length and prompt type, and qualitative visualizations, demonstrating effort in evaluation.
Code and supplementary materials are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The claimed 'personalization' is misleading: adaptation is performed independently per video (transductive test-time adaptation) and reset afterward, not accumulated across multiple videos of the same subject. This is standard per-instance TTA, not subject-level personalization as framed.

The interpretability claim regarding AU alignment is not quantitatively validated; only qualitative comparisons with OpenFace are shown. No ground-truth AU annotations are used to measure whether the learned AU prompts actually correspond to muscle activations.

The entropy-minimization adaptation on the same test video can overfit to that video, leading to suspiciously perfect scores (e.g., 100% WAR/F1 on some subjects in BioVid). This raises concerns about whether the reported gains reflect true generalization or memorization of the test sample.

Comparison with image-based TTA methods (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA) adapted to video may be unfair, as these methods do not exploit temporal dynamics and likely underperform due to their image-centric design. A stronger video-specific TTA baseline is missing.
The AU prompt set includes non-AU facial behaviors (e.g., head turn, eye gaze direction), which dilutes the 'Action Unit' claim and may confuse the model's semantic alignment.

The temporal window selection based on lowest entropy is a simple confidence-based heuristic, not a novel technical contribution. Its effectiveness is not deeply analyzed beyond ablation on window length.
The paper does not discuss ethical implications or privacy concerns of emotion recognition, which is important for real-world deployment, especially in healthcare contexts.
The method still requires training an AU adapter, temporal module, and classifier on source data, which is a form of fine-tuning, contradicting the abstract's claim of 'without CLIP fine-tuning'.

strengths: Introduces CLIP-AU and CLIP-AUTT, using Action Unit (AU) textual prompts within CLIP to model fine-grained facial muscle activations for subtle emotion recognition without AU labels or LLM-generated prompts.

CLIP-AUTT proposes an entropy-guided temporal window selection and AU prompt tuning strategy for subject-specific test-time personalization, which is well motivated for temporally evolving subtle expressions.

Extensive experiments on BioVid, StressID, and BAH show consistent improvements over CLIP-based FER and TTA baselines, with particularly strong gains on BioVid and StressID (e.g., CLIP-AUTT improves StressID F1 from 59.4 to 77.9).
Ablation studies on temporal module design, prompt template selection, window length, AU vs. class prompts, and AU adapter effectiveness provide useful insights into the method's behavior.
The approach is lightweight and computationally efficient, keeping CLIP encoders frozen and training only small adapters/modules, which is practical for personalized video-based emotion recognition.
Code is included in the supplementary materials, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Lack of explicit AU supervision or quantitative grounding: the AU similarity vectors are not validated against human-annotated AUs; the qualitative OpenFace comparison is insufficient to substantiate claims of interpretable AU semantics, and the model may simply learn prompt-specific features rather than true AU activations.

The test-time adaptation component is not isolated: TTA baselines are applied to a standard fine-tuned CLIP backbone, whereas CLIP-AUTT starts from the stronger CLIP-AU model. Applying TTA methods such as TPT or PromptAlign on top of CLIP-AU is missing, so the gain attributed to the proposed TTA cannot be cleanly disentangled from CLIP-AU pretraining.

On the BAH dataset, performance is weak: UAR is near chance (50.2%) and the F1 improvement over T3AL is marginal (41.1 vs. 40.7), which undercuts broad claims of robust personalization for ambivalent/hesitant expressions.
No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported; subject-wise results show high variance, and the fixed target subject sets could overstate the robustness of the method.

Entropy minimization on a single selected temporal window may amplify confirmation bias or overfit to transient cues; the paper provides limited empirical stability analysis, regularization, or failure-case discussion for this adaptation strategy.
Some entries in the 46 'AU' prompt list are not true facial action units (e.g., head turn, eye turn), which may dilute the physiological grounding and interpretability claims.
Related source-free and multi-source domain adaptation personalization methods for FER are discussed but not compared against, despite being directly relevant to the claimed personalization setting.

strengths: The paper introduces a lightweight and intuitive use of Action Unit (AU) textual prompts within a frozen CLIP framework, avoiding AU annotations and LLM-generated prompt supervision.
CLIP-AUTT combines entropy-guided temporal window selection with AU prompt tuning, providing a plausible and computationally efficient test-time personalization mechanism for video FER.
Experiments cover three challenging video emotion datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH) and compare against multiple CLIP-based FER and test-time adaptation baselines, with subject-wise analysis.
Ablations examine temporal window length, AU prompts versus class prompts, individual components, robustness to target-subject count, and prompt design, supporting the main design choices.
Efficiency is analyzed in terms of throughput, trainable parameters, and GFLOPs, showing a favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoff relative to competing methods.
The motivation is clear: subtle expressions are subject-specific and low-intensity, making personalization and fine-grained AU-like cues a sensible direction for healthcare-related FER.
Qualitative visualizations attempt to connect selected temporal windows and predicted AU activations to external OpenFace estimates, adding some interpretability evidence.
weaknesses: The AU prompt list is not faithful to standard FACS: it includes non-AU actions such as head turns/eye movements and several mislabeled or mistyped AUs (e.g., AU26 described as eye closure, AU28 as blink, AU25 with a malformed description), which undermines the claimed interpretable AU semantics.

There is no quantitative AU supervision or AU detection evaluation; the AU adapter and classifier are trained only with emotion classification loss, so the learned prompt embeddings are not shown to correspond to actual AUs. The interpretability claim rests mainly on qualitative OpenFace comparisons.

The test-time adaptation protocol is ambiguous: the text states adaptation is performed independently per subject video and reset afterward, while elsewhere it is described as subject-level personalization. If adaptation is per video, the method is sample-wise transductive TTA rather than subject-level personalization, which weakens the main contribution claim.

Hyperparameters such as temporal window length appear to be selected using target-set performance (e.g., Table 4 on BioVid), without a clear target-label-free validation protocol. This raises concerns about test-time label leakage.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing: several TTA baselines are image-level methods initialized from a source-fine-tuned CLIP rather than their standard zero-shot setting, and personalization/source-free adaptation methods cited in the related work are not empirically compared.

The code link appears absent or incomplete, and reproducibility details are limited: exact source/target splits, training choices, target-subject adaptation procedure, and hyperparameter selection are not sufficiently specified.

Entropy minimization on a single selected window with a frozen classifier can overfit to that window and produce overconfident but incorrect predictions; there is little regularization or failure-case analysis, and BAH UAR remains near chance (~50%).

The paper contains several typos and inconsistencies (e.g., WR vs WAR, PI vs F1, confusing reference to EmoCLIP† vs CLIP-ViT-B/32†), which reduce clarity and make some reported comparisons harder to verify.

strengths: Targets an important and challenging problem: subject-specific and fine-grained video emotion recognition, where personalization is meaningful.
Combines AU textual prompts with a frozen CLIP backbone and a lightweight temporal module, avoiding full CLIP fine-tuning and LLM-generated supervision.
Proposes a test-time adaptation scheme with entropy-guided window selection and AU prompt tuning; the approach is efficient in trainable parameters and computation.
Evaluates on three challenging datasets and includes subject-wise results, ablations, efficiency analysis, and some qualitative AU visualization.
The high-level motivation for AU-level semantics and test-time personalization is plausible and clearly explained in the introduction.
weaknesses: The AU prompt list in the supplementary is anatomically incorrect relative to FACS. For example, AU04 is listed as upper eyelids lifted, but FACS AU04 is brow lowerer; AU06 is listed as eyelids tightened, but AU06 is cheek raiser; AU12 is listed as cheek dimples/lip corners tightened, but AU12 is lip corner puller; AU25 is listed as narrow eye opening, but AU25 is lips part; AU26 is listed as eyes fully closed, but AU26 is jaw drop. Since AU semantics are the central claimed contribution, this error undermines the scientific validity and interpretability of the method.

There is no quantitative validation that the learned AU-video similarity vectors correspond to true AU activations. The only external check is a qualitative comparison with OpenFace on selected examples; no AU detection metrics, correlation, or subject-level AU agreement are reported. Without such validation, the model may simply learn arbitrary prompt-derived features rather than AU-aligned representations.

Personalization implementation is ambiguous and potentially contradictory. The main text says adaptation is reset after each video, which would not personalize across a subject, while the supplement describes subject-level adaptation. If multiple videos per subject exist, the method must either share adapted prompts across videos, making it order-dependent and transductive, or reset per video, which is not subject-level personalization.

Entropy-guided window selection relies on the model's own confidence and can reinforce overconfident wrong predictions under domain shift. There is no ground-truth peak-expression validation or comparison to motion/expression-based selection. The ablation shows only modest gains for window selection alone (0.7 WAR and 0.4 F1), yet the paper emphasizes it heavily.

Baseline comparisons appear unfair or unclear. The TTA baselines are described as using a CLIP-ViT-B/32† model fine-tuned on source data, while CLIP-AUTT builds on CLIP-AU. If CLIP-AUTT benefits from AU pretraining plus test-time adaptation while baselines only adapt a generic fine-tuned CLIP, the comparison conflates representation and adaptation. Missing FER/SFDA personalization baselines cited in related work further weaken the empirical case.

Statistical evidence is weak. Main results are averaged over only 10 target subjects with no confidence intervals or significance tests; only a supplementary subset reports three seeds. Several per-subject results are perfect or near-perfect, while others are near chance, suggesting high variance and possible selection or overfitting effects.

The reported gains on BAH are marginal and do not clearly support state-of-the-art personalization: WAR improves from 67.9 to 69.8 over T3AL and F1 from 40.7 to 41.1, while UAR remains around chance in the supplement. This limits the practical significance of the claims.

The paper has clarity and reproducibility issues. The code link appears missing in the manuscript; AU names contain typos such as eyes_elitted_narrow_eye_opening and lip_hite; equations and notation are occasionally inconsistent; and the main text misattributes a result by stating that EmoCLIP† is slightly higher in WAR (67.0 vs 66.5), while 67.0 is CLIP-ViT-B/32† in Table 1.

Novelty is limited relative to the claims. AU text prompts, lightweight adapters, temporal convolutional aggregation, and entropy-minimization prompt tuning are individually established; the paper mainly combines them. The specific technical advance over prior CLIP prompt tuning or AU-aware FER is not clearly isolated.

The test-time objective has no anti-collapse or trust-region mechanism, and the paper does not analyze whether adapting only AU embeddings can cause prompt collapse or degenerate solutions on a single selected window. The class-prompt ablation even shows TTA collapse on StressID with generic class prompts, suggesting the procedure is brittle and AU prompts may function mainly as a better initialization.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated and original use of Action Units as structured textual prompts for CLIP-based fine-grained facial expression recognition, avoiding LLM-generated prompts and AU annotations while remaining lightweight.

CLIP-AUTT introduces a sensible video test-time personalization approach combining entropy-guided temporal window selection with AU prompt tuning, enabling subject-specific adaptation without labels and with few trainable parameters.

The empirical study is broad: three challenging video ER datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH), multiple CLIP-based FER and TTA baselines, subject-wise personalization results, robustness analyses, and extensive ablations on components, window length, prompt design, and temporal module choice.

Performance gains are substantial on BioVid and StressID, especially in F1, and the paper provides useful qualitative analyses (OpenFace agreement, temporal window visualization, t-SNE) supporting the claimed benefits of AU prompting and test-time adaptation.
The paper is generally clear, well-organized, and includes implementation details and supplementary material that improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: Fairness of the TTA comparison is not fully controlled: CLIP-AUTT is built on the stronger CLIP-AU backbone with AU prompts and a temporal module, while most TTA baselines are image-level methods applied to a different base model. This confounds the effect of the proposed TTA strategy with the effect of the AU/temporal representation.

The AU interpretability claim is not quantitatively verified. The datasets lack AU ground truth, and the validation is qualitative/OpenFace-based for a few examples; the method may not actually learn anatomically grounded AUs rather than a task-specific prompt embedding space.

BAH results are marginal (e.g., WAR 69.8 vs. 67.9, F1 41.1 vs. 40.7) and UAR is almost exactly chance (~50.2%), indicating poor minority/ambivalent-class recognition. Claims of state-of-the-art performance on BAH should be tempered accordingly.

The paper does not compare to recent subject-specific or source-free personalization methods for FER, despite personalization being a central contribution. Comparing only to TTA and CLIP-FER baselines is insufficient to establish the personalization advantage.

The test-time adaptation protocol is somewhat ambiguous: the main text suggests resetting parameters after each subject video, while the supplement describes subject-level adaptation. It is unclear whether adaptation truly personalizes across a subject's videos or is effectively per-video adaptation.

Several smaller issues remain: the code/link is not visible in the manuscript, AU prompt descriptions contain typos (e.g., 'lip_hite'), notation is inconsistent in Eq. 12, and there is no explicit limitations or societal-impact discussion for an emotion-recognition system used in health-related contexts.
